finding.claim: Password change has no current-password or re-authentication check and no CSRF protection, so a cross-site request carrying the victim's session cookie can set the password.
finding.source: Cross-site POST from attacker page using victim's session cookie.

trace.note: login_required only checks presence of uid in session
set_password called with fixed value, no request input or current password

finding.guards_checked: Session presence check only. No CSRF token, no current-password verification, no re-auth. SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE not set in this file; modern browser Lax default would block cross-site POST cookies, so exploitability depends on cookie SameSite configuration. Real set_password body is a stub (routes.py:52-53).

verdict.guard_found: No CSRF token check and no current-password or re-auth check in routes.py. The only check is login_required's session-presence test (routes.py:11-12). Nothing in the directory sets SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE or any cookie SameSite attribute, so the browser's default Lax handling is the only possible block, and it is not configured in this code.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: POST /settings/password at routes.py:41-42 is guarded only by the session-presence check at routes.py:11-12 and calls set_password with a fixed value at routes.py:44, and no CSRF or re-auth control exists in the code. Whether a cross-site POST carries the victim's session cookie depends on the cookie's SameSite setting, which is not in the available files, so exploitability cannot be decided here. verdict.reason: routes.py:44 passes the literal "hunter2" as the new password to set_password, and the only gate is the session check at routes.py:11-12, so any logged-in user who calls /settings/password sets the account to that fixed value.
